title: How to Estimate Rehab Costs: A Line-Item Method
metaDescription: How investors estimate rehab costs line by line: room-by-room walkthroughs, systems checks, contingency logic and the mistakes that blow up a rehab budget.
h1: How to Estimate Rehab Costs Line by Line
dek: A reliable rehab estimate is built line by line: every task gets a quantity, a unit, a labor cost and a material cost, grouped by trade and room. Contingency is then sized to the risks you could not see, not added as a flat cushion to cover guesswork.
keyTakeaways: A rehab estimate is a list of measured line items, each with a quantity, a unit of measure, labor, material and any disposal cost.
Estimators walk a house in a fixed order, systems first and finishes last, because systems problems change everything downstream.
Contingency should be sized to specific unknowns such as concealed plumbing, subfloor rot or old wiring, and it should be larger on older and vacant houses.
The most expensive estimating mistakes are omissions, not wrong unit prices: missed permits, missed debris removal, missed patching after trades.
An estimate is only as good as the scope behind it, so write the scope and the estimate together and price the same document contractors will bid.

sections.h2: What is a line-item rehab estimate?
sections.body:
A line-item rehab estimate breaks a renovation into individual tasks and prices each one separately. Instead of writing "kitchen remodel" with a single number beside it, you write out every piece of work the kitchen needs: demolition of existing cabinets and counters, haul-off, any drywall replacement, rough plumbing changes, electrical circuits for appliances, new base and wall cabinets, countertops, backsplash, sink and faucet, appliance installation, lighting, flooring, trim and paint.

Each line carries five things: a description specific enough that two contractors would price the same work, a quantity, a unit of measure (each, linear foot, square foot, square, opening, fixture), a labor component and a material component. Many estimators add a sixth column for disposal or a note on who supplies the material.

The point of this level of detail is not paperwork. It is what lets you compare bids honestly, cut scope without guessing what you removed, track draws against completed work, and catch the line a contractor quietly left out. A lump-sum number can be right by accident. A line-item estimate is right because each piece of it was checked.

Line-item estimates also make finish-level decisions visible. When a kitchen is broken into cabinets, tops, backsplash and hardware, you can see exactly where a rental-grade choice differs from a flip-grade choice and price both versions side by side. That is how a professional estimator can hand an investor two or three plans for the same house and let the after-repair value decide which one is worth building.

sections.h2: What order should you walk a house in?
sections.body:
Experienced estimators walk every house in roughly the same order, because problems found early change the scope of everything found later.

Start outside. Look at the roof covering, flashing, gutters and downspouts, then grading and drainage away from the foundation. Walk the perimeter looking at siding, trim, windows, doors and any sign of soft wood. Note the driveway, walks, steps, railings and fencing. Look at the electric service entrance and the meter base, and find the water shutoff and the gas meter.

Then go down, not up. The basement or crawlspace tells you about the foundation, the framing, the water history of the house, the drain lines, the supply piping, the water heater, the furnace or boiler and often the electrical panel. A wet basement, a sagging beam or a panel nobody will insure changes the budget more than any finish choice.

After the structure and systems, work through the living space room by room in a consistent direction so you never skip a room. Finish with the attic, where you check insulation depth, ventilation, roof decking from below, signs of past leaks and any wiring that runs through it.

Writing the estimate in the same order you walked keeps it organized and makes it easier for a contractor to follow. It also helps you notice when something is missing. If the walkthrough sheet has a heading for the attic and nothing under it, you know you did not look.

sections.h2: What estimators check in the major systems
sections.body:
Systems are where budgets go wrong, so estimators look at them before they look at a single cabinet.

Electrical: panel brand and condition, service size, whether the panel has open slots, double-tapped breakers, aluminum branch wiring, ungrounded two-wire circuits, knob-and-tube in older houses, missing GFCI and AFCI protection where current code requires it, and smoke and carbon monoxide detection. A panel that a home inspector or insurer will flag is an automatic line item.

Plumbing: supply material (copper, galvanized steel, CPVC, PEX, polybutylene), drain material (cast iron, galvanized, ABS, PVC, clay or Orangeburg at the sewer), visible leaks, water pressure at the farthest fixture, the age and venting of the water heater, and whether the main sewer line needs a camera inspection. Galvanized supply and older cast-iron drains are frequent sources of mid-project surprises.

HVAC: equipment age and data plate, heat exchanger condition on older furnaces, evidence of a cracked heat exchanger or rollout, condition of ductwork, return air sizing, condensate drainage and the condition of the condenser outside. Boiler systems get a separate look at piping, radiators and expansion tanks.

Structure and envelope: foundation cracks and their pattern, floor deflection, rot at sills and rim joists, roof age and layers, attic ventilation, window condition and any sign of water intrusion.

For each system, the estimate should say clearly if the plan is to repair, replace or leave it alone, and why. "HVAC: service and certify, existing equipment functional" is a decision. A blank line is a risk.

sections.h2: Room-by-room: what goes on the estimate
sections.body:
Once systems are settled, the interior estimate follows a repeatable pattern in every room.

Kitchens: cabinets (repair, reface, paint or replace), countertops by linear foot or square foot, backsplash by square foot, sink and faucet, disposal, appliance package, dedicated circuits, range hood venting, lighting, flooring, and any wall changes. Note whether the layout stays the same, because moving plumbing or gas is a different estimate.

Bathrooms: tub or shower (reglaze, liner, retile or replace), valve replacement, vanity and top, toilet, mirror and lighting, exhaust fan ducted to the exterior, floor tile or LVP, subfloor condition around the toilet and tub, accessories, and caulk and paint.

Bedrooms and living areas: flooring by square foot, drywall or plaster repair, paint by room or by square foot of wall, doors and hardware, closet systems, window treatments if included, outlets and switches, light fixtures and ceiling fans.

Whole-house lines that often get missed: interior doors and trim as a group, smoke and CO detectors, outlet and switch replacement throughout, light fixture packages, final cleaning, lockbox and rekey, and permit fees.

Exterior lines: roof, gutters, siding or masonry repair, exterior paint, windows, entry doors, garage door, concrete, landscaping cleanup and tree work.

A practical habit is to measure every room once and record floor area, wall perimeter and ceiling height. Those three numbers drive flooring, baseboard, paint and drywall quantities, and you will not have to go back to the property to recalculate them.

sections.h2: How to price labor and materials without guessing
sections.body:
Unit pricing is where most new investors focus, but it is the part of estimating that improves most easily with practice and good records.

Separate labor from material on every line. Material costs move with supply and the finish level you choose, while labor moves with local market conditions and the difficulty of the specific house. Keeping them apart lets you update one without rebuilding the whole estimate.

Build your own price book. Every time a bid comes in or an invoice is paid, record the unit cost for each line by market. Over time your price book becomes the single most valuable estimating tool you own, far better than national cost guides, because it reflects the trades you actually hire in the areas where you actually buy.

Adjust for difficulty. The same line item costs more in a house with plaster walls, a crawlspace with little clearance, a third-floor bathroom or no off-street parking for the dumpster. Note those conditions on the estimate so the difficulty adjustment is visible instead of buried.

Price the whole task, not just the headline item. A new toilet line should include the wax ring, supply line and haul-away of the old fixture. A flooring line should include underlayment, transitions, shoe molding and moving appliances.

When you request contractor bids, send the same line-item scope to every bidder. Their numbers become directly comparable, and the gaps between them tell you where a bidder either misunderstood the work or is pricing a risk you missed.

sections.h2: How much contingency should a rehab estimate carry?
sections.body:
Contingency is money set aside for work you could not see or confirm during the walkthrough. It is not a cushion for sloppy estimating, and it should not be a fixed number applied to every house.

The right way to size contingency is to list the specific unknowns and ask how likely each one is and what it would cost if it turned out badly. Common unknowns include concealed plumbing inside walls, subfloor rot under tubs and toilets, rot behind siding or at window sills, knob-and-tube wiring that only appears when walls are opened, a sewer lateral that has not been scoped, hidden mold behind finished basement walls, and structural issues that cosmetic finishes have covered.

Some conditions call for more contingency:
- Older houses, especially pre-war construction with plaster, original wiring and galvanized or cast-iron piping.
- Vacant and bank-owned properties, which may have freeze damage, missing components or systems that cannot be tested until utilities are on.
- Projects that open walls extensively, because each opened wall is a chance to find something.
- Houses where you could not access an area such as an attic, crawlspace or locked unit.

Other conditions justify less: a newer house, systems already tested under power and water, a cosmetic-only scope, or a sewer line that has already been camera-inspected.

The best way to shrink contingency is to remove unknowns before you buy. Getting utilities turned on, running water through every fixture, camera-scoping the sewer and pulling a few outlet covers costs very little compared to discovering those problems after closing. Treat contingency as the price of what you still do not know.

sections.h2: The line items investors forget most often
sections.body:
Most blown rehab budgets do not come from wrong unit prices. They come from lines that were never on the estimate. These are the omissions that show up again and again:

- Permits and plan review fees, plus the time and trips needed for inspections.
- Dumpsters and debris haul-off, often more than one load on a full gut.
- Drywall patching and paint touch-up after electricians and plumbers open walls.
- Subfloor repair under old tile, toilets and tubs.
- Code-triggered upgrades: smoke and CO detectors, GFCI and AFCI protection, handrails and guardrails, egress in basement bedrooms.
- Lead-safe work practices on pre-1978 houses when painted surfaces are disturbed.
- Utility reconnection, meter work, and gas line pressure testing on vacant homes.
- Appliance delivery and installation, plus connection parts.
- Rekeying or new locks, mailbox, house numbers and doorbell.
- Final construction cleaning and window cleaning before listing or leasing.
- Exterior cleanup: overgrown landscaping, tree limbs over the roof, junk in the yard or garage.
- Carrying costs during the rehab, which belong in the deal analysis even if they are not construction lines.

A simple defense is a master checklist you run against every estimate before you finalize it. If a line does not apply, mark it as not applicable rather than leaving it off. That small habit forces you to consider every item on every house.

sections.h2: Turning the estimate into a scope, a budget and a draw schedule
sections.body:
A finished estimate does three jobs, and it should be written so it can do all of them.

First, it is the basis of the scope of work contractors will bid. That means descriptions need to be specific about materials, quantities and locations. "Replace flooring" is not biddable. "Install LVP in living room, dining room, hall and three bedrooms, with underlayment, transitions and new shoe molding" is.

Second, it is the project budget you track against. Every change order, every overrun and every saving should be recorded against the original line so you can see where the house differed from your walkthrough. Over many projects, those differences are exactly what tighten your future estimates.

Third, it is the foundation of the draw schedule. Lenders and investors release construction money as work is completed, and a draw schedule groups line items into stages such as demolition, rough-ins, inspections passed, drywall, finishes and final. If the estimate is organized by trade and room, building the draw schedule is a matter of grouping lines. If it is a lump sum, nobody can tell what has been earned.

This is why Genstone Construction delivers its estimates as a detailed scope with labor, materials and a draw schedule rather than a single number, and why its Pre-Offer Rehab Review is built to test whether the repair budget supports the offer before an investor commits capital. Whoever prepares your estimate, ask for that same structure. It is the difference between a budget you can manage and a number you hope holds.

sections.h2: How to check your own estimate before you buy
sections.body:
Before an estimate goes into an offer, run it through a few checks.

Compare it to the after-repair value plan. Every major line should support the finish level the comparable sales require. If the comps show updated kitchens and your estimate paints the existing cabinets, either the ARV is too high or the kitchen line is too low.

Check it against the house's age. A pre-war house with no electrical, plumbing or contingency lines is almost certainly under-scoped. A newer house with a full rewire line probably needs a second look.

Look for missing rooms. Count the rooms on the estimate and compare to the listing and your floor plan notes. Laundry rooms, half baths, stairways, porches and garages are easy to skip.

Read it as a contractor would. If you handed this document to a contractor who had never seen the house, could they price it without calling you? Every question they would need to ask is a line that needs more detail.

Finally, get a second opinion on anything structural, anything involving a sewer line and any major system you could not test. A small inspection fee before closing is the least expensive contingency there is.

faqs.q: What is the most accurate way to estimate rehab costs?
faqs.a: The most accurate method is a line-item estimate built from a full walkthrough, with every task listed by trade and room and priced with a quantity, unit, labor cost and material cost. Accuracy improves further when you test systems under power and water, camera-scope the sewer, and price lines from your own record of past bids in that market rather than national averages. Shortcuts like cost per square foot are useful for screening deals but not for committing to an offer.

faqs.q: Should I use a cost per square foot to estimate a rehab?
faqs.a: Cost per square foot is useful only as a quick screening tool when you are deciding whether a property deserves a walkthrough. It hides the factors that drive rehab cost: the number of kitchens and baths, the condition of the systems, the age of the house and how much of it needs to be opened up. Two houses of the same size can have very different budgets. Once you are serious about an offer, replace the rough number with a line-item estimate.

faqs.q: How do I decide how much contingency to include?
faqs.a: List the specific things you could not confirm during the walkthrough, such as concealed plumbing, subfloor condition, wiring behind plaster or an unscoped sewer line, then judge how likely and how costly each one is. Older homes, vacant or bank-owned homes and scopes that open many walls warrant more contingency. Newer homes with tested systems and cosmetic scopes warrant less. The most effective way to reduce contingency is to remove unknowns with inexpensive checks before you buy.

faqs.q: Why do contractor bids vary so much on the same house?
faqs.a: Bids vary mostly because contractors are pricing different scopes, not because some are honest and others are not. When a bidder works from a vague description, each one fills in the gaps with their own assumptions about materials, quantities and what is included. Sending every bidder the same detailed line-item scope makes their numbers comparable, and the remaining differences usually reveal a misunderstanding or a risk one contractor saw that the others did not.

faqs.q: What should a professional rehab estimate include?
faqs.a: A professional rehab estimate should list each task with a description, quantity, unit of measure, labor cost and material cost, organized by trade or room. It should state which systems are being repaired, replaced or left as-is, include permits, debris removal and cleaning, identify contingency separately, and ideally group lines into a draw schedule tied to completed stages of work. Some estimators also provide alternate finish levels so the scope can be matched to the after-repair value.
